newsitem.title: CHINA: Chinese yuan seen stable in 1997 - bank official.
newsitem.headline: Chinese yuan seen stable in 1997 - bank official.

text.p: The Chinese yuan will be stable in a range between 8.27 and 8.31 against the U.S. dollar in 1997, with demand for the dollar rising after steady gains in the yuan in the past three years, bank officials said on Friday.

Domestic Chinese demand for foreign currency will increase in 1997 as the Chinese economy enters a new cycle of high growth, imports recover and foreign investment remains at current levels, Li Xuping, an official of state-run Shanghai Pudong Development Bank, said.
Speaking at a foreign currency risk management seminar in Shanghai, Li said: "The yuan's movements will remain stable in 1997, mainly between 8.27 and 8.31 against the U.S. dollar.".
Rises in the Chinese yuan since 1994, when Beijing unified its dual currency system, were mainly due to the growth of foreign investment in China, Li said.
By the end of 1996, the yuan had risen to 8.2984 against the U.S. dollar, from 8.7000 at the beginning of 1994, he said.
Direct foreign investment in China hit $42.3 billion in 1996, up from $33.9 billion in 1994, he said.

In 1997, China's central bank would buy more foreign currency to maintain high foreign reserves -- currently the highest in the world at $105 billion -- to help stablise Hong Kong's financial markets, Li said.
Hong Kong reverts from British to Chinese rule on July 1 this year.

Li said the Chinese yuan was still a long way from being a fully market-driving currency. The People's Bank of China, the central bank, was the only net buyer of the yuan on China's foreign exchange market while state-run banks remained net sellers, he said.
